catalog_quote: The system that exists throughout LC is one of two basic tones, High ... and Low ..., which may combine on a given syllable (with restricted and varying distribution) to give Falling (H+L ...), and less frequently, Rising (L+H ...) tones. Faraclas (1984a,b) argues that for Obolo, there is a third contrastive tone, which he calls Extra-high. In addition to these two basic tones, there is also a phonologically significant Downstep (Ds = !); i.e., the non-predictable lowering of H following another H, which has the effect of lowering the 'ceiling' for subsequent H tone realization. Lower Cross languages can therefore be characterized as being two-toned, terraced level languages. [p.47] ... new_statements.quote: Lower Cross languages can therefore be characterized as being two-toned, terraced level languages. [p.47] ... it is difficult to find any true evidence for stress, at least in the sense proposed by Ward [p.55]. [fn.32:] This is not to assert that there is no stress at all in Efik or the other LC languages. There is likely some sort phrasal stress, and also the juncture between elements of compound words appears to be marked by stress, but these are clearly not what Ward was referring to. Faraclas (1984b) presents an analysis of Obolo incorporating phrasal stress.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Enwang, like all Lower Cross languages in Connell's survey, is a two-tone (H/L) terraced-level tone language with contrastive downstep; Connell finds no real evidence for lexical word stress (Ward's verb-root stress claim for Efik is rejected), and allows only that some phrasal stress and stress at compound-internal junctures probably exist; he refers to Efik/LC as 'a non-stress language'. No word-stress position is stated for Enwang or any LC language.
new_statements.exceptions: None for Enwang. Faraclas (1984b) is cited as analysing Obolo (another LC language) with phrasal stress and an extra-high tone; the group-level claim is explicitly a broad outline, and Connell's Enwang data were not cross-checked with speakers (p.11).
new_statements.domain_note: Group-level statement about Lower Cross as a whole, argued mainly on Efik data (Ward 1933, Cook 1985); Enwang is covered only as one of the 19 languages sampled. Tone claim stated to hold 'at least.. of lexical items in citation form' (p.47). Stress remarks concern word vs phrase: no word-level stress evidence; phrasal and compound-juncture stress 'likely'.
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog enwa1245 'Enwan (Akwa Ibom State)' [enw] = Connell's 'Enwang' (Mbo LGA; Enwang-Uda subgroup enwa1244, mutually intelligible with Uda udaa1238). Do not confuse with the Edoid Enwan [env] of Edo State (Sasaru-Enwan-Igwe). The quoted statement is a Lower Cross group-level claim (19 languages sampled, evidence drawn mainly from Efik), not an Enwang-specific description; Connell notes his Enwang data were not cross-checked with speakers.

sources.note: Sec. 3.3 p.10: 'in all languages of the group, there are two tones, high (H) and low (L), and contrastive downstep (D) which operates on H tones'. Sec. 5 p.12: 'Tonal systems in the group appear to be further complicated through interaction with phrasal stress, but except for Faraclas (1984b) for Obolo, no investigation in this area has been done.' Enwang: 15,000 speakers (p.5), consonant inventory (p.7), Enwang-Uda proposed as a minor subgroup. No word-stress statement.
